prize_parts.citation: For the invention of the optical lattice clock and its development to a fractional uncertainty at the 10^-18 level

statement.case_for: My preferred configuration is unchanged: B029, credited to Katori and Ye. After the full first round I find the case stronger, not weaker, because the objections raised against it have narrowed to one question, whether it is a separate achievement from the 2005 and 2012 prizes. I think it is. The 2005 prize honoured the frequency comb and comb-based precision spectroscopy; the comb is how an optical frequency is counted, not what makes a clock accurate. The 2012 prize honoured the control and measurement of individual quantum systems, including single trapped ions. The lattice clock solves a different problem, which is to interrogate a very large number of neutral atoms at once, with the Doppler and recoil shifts removed by confinement, while the trap does not perturb the clock transition. That is the magic-wavelength idea, which Katori proposed. Ye's group then demonstrated what the idea makes possible: strontium lattice clocks whose systematic uncertainty reached the 10^-18 level, with measurements that exposed blackbody, many-body collisional and gravitational-redshift effects within a millimetre-scale sample. I would build the citation on those two things only, the invention and the demonstrated performance, and not on a future redefinition of the second or on any as-yet-unmade discovery about constants. The result has been reproduced and intercompared in laboratories with no link to JILA, and the physics is concrete and checkable. I did not hear any argument in round 1 that changes my reading of the science.
statement.case_against: The overlap argument is legitimate and I do not dismiss it. Hall and Haensch (2005) and Wineland and Haroche (2012) are close relatives, and an Al+ ion clock reached comparable accuracy, so a reader could see the lattice clock as the next step in one family. I answer that the scheme is different in kind, but I accept the reasonable disagreement among colleagues, notably Eriksson and Mehlig, who weight the comparison more heavily. The second weakness is that the record number is not unique: Lemonde, Ludlow, Lisdat, Hinkley, Bloom and others, and the ion-clock groups, reached comparable accuracy, so a two-name prize inevitably leaves out real contributors. I think that is acceptable only if the citation names the concept and its realisation rather than a record. Third, the practical consequences are prospective: no clock comparison has yet found a violation of a constant, and the redefinition of the second has not been decided. I do not count either of those against the science, but they mean the case rests on demonstrated capability.

responses.point: Danielsson holds B012, the experimental discovery of the Higgs boson, credited to Della Negra, Jenni and Virdee, and grants that B029 is a strong alternative with cleaner attribution but regards the Higgs as an actual discovery about nature while the clock payoff is still prospective.
responses.response: I agree on the weight of the discovery, and I do not want to argue that a clock is more important than the Higgs boson. The question for a prize is whether the credited names and the citation fit the achievement. Here I side with Eriksson, Kroll and Pearce: two collaborations of thousands made the discovery, and a citation for the conception and leadership of the experiments rewards something other than the discovery as the physics community understands it. You say yourself that spokespersons at the time of discovery, detector pioneers and accelerator leaders have comparable claims. I would want a stated principle for choosing three from that set, and none has been offered. I would reconsider if it could be shown that one or two of the three made a decisive individual contribution to the discovery itself, not to building the apparatus. I also disagree that the clock case is only prospective: its merit is the invention and the 10^-18 demonstration, both done and independently confirmed, and that is the sense in which I call it a discovery-level result in measurement.

responses.point: Eriksson prefers B035 (DMFT), now says he ranked B029 too low and would support it as a prize, while maintaining that DMFT is the more fundamental idea, and that the 1e-18 result rests on many clock groups and on precision metrology following the 2005 and 2012 prizes.
responses.response: Thank you for the candour. I accept that DMFT is a deep idea, and I accept your correction that I understated how many clock groups stand near the 10^-18 milestone. That is why I now want the citation to name the lattice clock and its development, with no record number in it, and why I regard the omission of other groups as a limit on the prize rather than something to hide. On the 2005 overlap, I would put it this way for the committee: the comb is a readout tool for optical clocks of every type, so a clock prize does not duplicate it, just as the 2005 prize did not duplicate the atomic-clock work that came before it. The conceptually new step in B029 is magic-wavelength confinement, which is unrelated to the comb. I agree with you on B035 that Metzner's omission cannot be solved by redrafting a three-name set without leaving out someone whose contribution is documented, so I treat it as the deciding obstacle there and not as a footnote.

responses.point: Kroll ranks B029 first, writes new tests of fundamental physics and a path to redefining the second into his citation, and discloses a research stay in John Hall's laboratory at Boulder as a perceived connection to Ye.
responses.response: I appreciate that you recorded the Hall connection, and I think disclosure is the right treatment. It is not grounds for recusal. You claim no collaboration, supervision or shared funding with Ye or Katori. The science does not depend on JILA, and the committee's support for B029 does not depend on your view: Johansson, Mehlig, Olsson, Pearce and I reached it independently, and I ranked it first before reading anyone else's round-1 statement. I do disagree with part of your citation wording. I would not put new tests of fundamental physics or the redefinition of the second into the citation, because both are prospective and the second is not decided; if either arrives, it will arrive because the clocks were already achieved. A citation that is limited to the invention and the demonstrated precision is the one I can defend if the outcome of those tests turns out to be null.

responses.point: Johansson moved from B018 to B029 after the opening ballots, places B018 behind the clocks because of the overlap with 2012, and wants the pending redefinition of the second kept out of the merits.
responses.response: I agree with each of those reservations about B018, and I share your reluctance to base the clock case on the redefinition. Where I want to be careful is on the fallback. If B029 does not hold, I would not move automatically to B018. The Cirac-Zoller proposal is conceptually important, but the first ion-trap gate demonstrations came from the NIST group and from Monroe, who are not in the credited trio, and the gate work builds directly on what the 2012 prize honoured. I would want the committee to say precisely what the 2012 prize left over before choosing it. My real second choice remains B031, because the Bistritzer-MacDonald prediction preceded the 2018 experiments, which is a rare and clean pattern in condensed matter, but I agree with Eriksson and Danielsson that the origin of the correlated states is still unresolved, so it is a candidate for a later year rather than this one.

uncertainties: Whether the committee will accept that the lattice clock is a distinct achievement from the 2005 and 2012 prizes; I have argued it, but a reasonable member could weigh the overlap more heavily than I do.

Whether the exclusion of Lemonde, Ludlow, Lisdat, Hinkley and the Al+ ion-clock groups is acceptable in a two-name configuration; I judge it so only if the citation names the concept and its realisation, not the record.

How much the committee wants to rest on the redefinition of the second or on future tests of fundamental constants; I do not treat these as scientific evidence and my citation does not depend on them.
I have not independently verified the detailed team histories for B031 or B018 and am relying on my recollection of the literature for those comparisons.
I have no access to the later vote, so I cannot say whether my position will be shared by enough colleagues to prevail.
statement.conflict_note: No specific conflict with the proposed B029 laureates (Katori, Ye) is apparent from my provided profile. For disclosure: I have a long-running scientific collaboration with Anne L'Huillier and have collaborated with Ursula Keller's group at ETH Zurich; Andreas Wallraff (B004) is at ETH Zurich, which is institutional proximity but not a documented personal tie. None of this concerns my preferred configuration. I have noted Kroll's disclosure about the Hall laboratory and regard it as a disclosure only, not a reason for recusal.
